summary: Côte d'Ivoire lies on the Gulf of Guinea coast of West Africa, is the world's largest cocoa producer, and has Abidjan as its economic center.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced to the north in the 14th–15th centuries by Dyula merchants of the Mali Empire along the gold and kola nut trade routes, and the northern city of Kong was an important center of Islamic learning in the 17th–18th centuries. During the colonial period and after independence, large numbers of migrant workers from Mali, Burkina Faso and Guinea entered the cocoa and coffee plantations of the south, greatly increasing the proportion of Muslims. Today Muslims are concentrated mainly in the north and have formed large communities in the southern cities.

ranking.name: Protestantism and other Christian denominations
ranking.description: Protestantism and other Christian denominations arrived in the early 20th century; in 1913–1915 the Liberian prophet William Wadé Harris preached along the southern coast of Côte d'Ivoire, bringing tens of thousands to convert to Christianity and giving rise to the indigenous Harrist Church. Afterwards the Methodist, Pentecostal and Evangelical churches grew rapidly in the south, attracting large numbers of followers especially in cities such as Abidjan.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced in 1895 by missionaries of the Society of African Missions and developed with French colonial expansion; church schools trained many political elites, including the first president, Félix Houphouët-Boigny. Houphouët-Boigny built the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in his hometown of Yamoussoukro, which was consecrated by Pope John Paul II in 1990 and is one of the largest churches in the world.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population is about 13%, mainly young people living in cities, and people who, though belonging to no religious organization, move between traditional beliefs and Christianity. The civil war and political crises of 2002–2011 also led some people to distance themselves from religious organizations.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Traditional beliefs include ancestor worship, mask dances and secret societies, for example the Dan of the west, the Baoulé of the center and the Poro society of the Senufo of the north. Although only about 2% follow the traditional religion exclusively, many Christians and Muslims still take part in traditional rituals, and the art of masks and carving is also an important part of Ivorian culture.

religion.background: Before colonization, Côte d'Ivoire was home to many peoples, and religion centered on ancestor worship and nature beliefs. From the 14th century Islam arrived along the northern trade networks, Catholicism arrived after French colonization in the late 19th century, and in 1913 the preaching movement of the prophet Harris led large numbers of southern residents to convert to Christianity. After independence in 1960, the first president, Houphouët-Boigny, promoted religious tolerance, but in the political crises of the 2000s the controversy over 'Ivoirité' (Ivorian identity) heightened tension between northern Muslims and southern Christians. Today religion is broadly distributed as Muslims in the north and Christians in the south.

language.official: French is the official language, and there are about 70 indigenous languages.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French became the language of administration and education when France established the colony of Côte d'Ivoire in 1893, and remained the official language after independence in 1960. Because there are about 70 indigenous languages in the country, French has become the common language across ethnic groups, and Abidjan has even developed 'Ivorian French', mixed with indigenous vocabulary, and the slang 'Nouchi', so about one third of the population use French as their main language.

ranking.name: Baoulé
ranking.description: Baoulé is the language of the Baoulé people of the center, belongs to the Akan group, and is close to the language of the Asante of Ghana. It is said that in the 18th century Queen Abla Pokou of the Akan led her people west from Ghana and founded the Baoulé people. The Baoulé are the ethnic group of the first president, Houphouët-Boigny, and the capital, Yamoussoukro, lies in the Baoulé-speaking area.

ranking.name: Dyula
ranking.description: Dyula is a Mandingo language, originally the commercial language of Dyula merchants, which became popular in the northern and western cities with trans-regional trade. Because large numbers of migrant workers from Mali and Burkina Faso also use closely related languages, Dyula has become the common language among Muslims in the north and in cities, with a large number of second-language speakers.

language.history: Côte d'Ivoire has about 70 languages belonging to different branches such as Akan, Mande, Gur and Kru, reflecting its multi-ethnic history. From the 14th century the Dyula merchants of the Mande language family brought Dyula to the north, and in the 18th century the Baoulé of the Akan moved into the center from the east. After French colonization in 1893, French became the language of administration and education, and after independence in 1960 French remained the sole official language. The rapid urbanization of Abidjan in the late 20th century mixed French with indigenous languages, forming distinctive Ivorian French and Nouchi.

ranking.name: Attiéké
ranking.description: A granular staple made from grated, fermented and steamed cassava, with a texture like couscous and a slight sourness, often eaten with grilled fish, tomato and onion.
ranking.history: Attiéké originates from peoples along the southern lagoons such as the Adjoukrou and the Ebrié, and is a technique passed down by local women over generations, with a process of peeling, grating, fermenting, pressing dry and steaming. In the 20th century it spread across the country with the development of Abidjan, and eating it with grilled fish has become a national favorite. In 2024 UNESCO inscribed 'Knowledge and know-how of attiéké' on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

ranking.name: Alloco (fried plantain)
ranking.description: Ripe plantains are cut into pieces and deep-fried until golden and caramelized, crisp outside and soft inside with a sweet taste, often eaten with chili sauce, onion or grilled fish.
ranking.history: Plantains are native to Southeast Asia and are generally thought to have reached Africa more than a thousand years ago through Indian Ocean trade, and were later widely grown in the tropical areas of West Africa. Fried plantain is the most popular street snack in Côte d'Ivoire, the alloco stalls of Abidjan are very famous, and a gathering place of food stalls in the Cocody district is called the 'Allocodrome'. It is also an everyday family side dish, often served with chicken or fish.

ranking.name: Kedjenou
ranking.description: Chicken is placed in a sealed clay pot with tomato, onion, chili and spices, with no water added, and slowly simmered over low heat so that the chicken cooks in its own juices.
ranking.history: Kedjenou originates from the Baoulé people and is traditionally sealed in a clay pot (canari) set over charcoal; while cooking, the pot is simply shaken without being opened, preserving the original flavor of the ingredients. This waterless method of cooking is practical in rural areas short of water. Today it is regarded as one of the signature dishes of Côte d'Ivoire and often appears at festivals, weddings and when entertaining guests.

ranking.name: Foutou
ranking.description: Cooked cassava, plantain or yam is pounded with a pestle in a wooden mortar into an elastic dough, eaten with peanut sauce or palm sauce.
ranking.history: Foutou is a staple shared across West and Central Africa, and 'foutou' is the French spelling used in Côte d'Ivoire. Pounding foutou takes great strength and is traditionally done cooperatively by the women of the household, and the sound of pestle on mortar is a daily scene of village life. Foutou made from plantain ('foutou banane') is especially popular in Côte d'Ivoire and is often eaten with palm sauce (sauce graine).

ranking.name: Sauce arachide (peanut sauce)
ranking.description: A thick stew of peanut butter, tomato, onion and chicken or fish, with a rich, mellow texture and peanut aroma, often eaten with rice or foutou.
ranking.history: Peanuts are native to South America and were brought to West Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century, and are widely grown in the savanna region of northern Côte d'Ivoire. Peanut stew is common throughout West Africa under various names, such as Mali's 'tigadèguèna'. In Côte d'Ivoire it is one of the most common sauces of everyday family meals, especially served with rice.
